desc:
Looking at a binary tree from below, each vertical line shows only the lowest node on it. Return the values of the visible nodes ordered from the leftmost column to the rightmost column.

Give every node a column: the root is in column 0, the left child of a node in column c is in column c - 1 and its right child is in column c + 1. Imagine every column as a vertical line.

In each column, the visible node is the one furthest from the root (largest level). If two nodes of one column are on the same, deepest, level, the right one is visible (it comes last in level order). The empty tree gives [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] column 0 contains the nodes 1, 5 and 6; the nodes 5 and 6 are both on the deepest level of that column, and 6 is the right one. The answer is [4, 2, 6, 3, 7].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Again you need the column of every node. What decides which node of a column is visible now?
The visible node is the last node of its column in level order: deeper levels come later, and on one level nodes come left to right.
While scanning the array in order, keep a dictionary column → value and overwrite it every time you see the column. Output the values sorted by column.
editorial: Mirror image of the top view logic. Scan the nodes in level order while propagating columns from parents to children (left child: column - 1, right child: column + 1). Because level order visits shallow nodes before deep ones and left nodes before right ones on a level, the last node written for a column is the deepest and, among the deepest, the rightmost, which is exactly the node that is visible from below.
So the only change relative to the top view is that every node overwrites the stored value instead of being ignored. The time is O(n) plus the output ordering over the (consecutive) columns.
